quotes.quote: Agra Marble Inlay is a fine example of craftsmanship, combining the beauty of marble with the allure of semi-precious stones.
Agra Marble Inlay technique is a time-honored art form that dates back to the Mughal era, with a rich tradition of craftsmanship centered around Agra, India.
One of them is Parchin Kari or Pachhikari. Parchin Kari is the art of inlaying coloured or semi-precious stones into a stone base, often in geometric or flower patterns.
called parchin kari or parchinkari (Persian: پرچین کاری) in the Indian subcontinent, is a term for the inlay technique of using cut and fitted, highly polished colored stones to create images.
In Mughal India, pietra dura was known as parchin kari, literally 'inlay' or 'driven-in' work.
which had been adapted into the local Mughal style and came to be known as parchin kari, literally meaning 'driven in'.
pietra dura, meaning "hard stone" in Italian, is a technique wherein precious and semi-precious stones are cut, polished and inlaid - generally on hard stone, such as marble - to represent an image.
This stonework is generally referred to as pietra dura ("hard stone" in Italian) and known as parchin kari in India.
Stone Inlay is also known as Parchin kari which is known as the most attractive and popular forms of Art in Agra.
As the Indian marble is one of the hardest materials to work, it is not an easy process. This work on stone is a combination of carving, inlaying, engraving and sculpture.
Parchin kari or the stone of semi-precious stones - agate, turquoise, cornelian, jasper, bloodstone, mother of pearl, malachite and lapis lazuli in marble is unique to Agra.
The famous stone Inlay work of Agra reflects the mosaic work (Pietra Dura) used in Taj Mahal and Fatehpur Sikri.
The craft flourished and reached its peak during the era of the Mughals in medieval India and especially after the construction of Taj Mahal.
a rich tradition of craftsmanship centered around Agra, India
Since the time of Shah Jahan, Agra in Uttar Pradesh has remained a thriving centre for marble work, including inlay.
It was made by craftsmen in Agra, a renowned centre for the inlaying of marble with semi-precious stones from the reign of Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658).
The sequence of processes that culminates in the realization of a masterpiece of marble stone was perfected by the artisans in the 17th century, and has remained largely unchanged for over 400 years.

It was built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal with construction starting in 1632 AD and completed in 1648 AD, with the mosque, the guest house and the main gateway on the south, the outer courtyard and its cloisters were added subsequently and completed in 1653 AD.
Begun in 1632, the entire complex was not completed until 1653
The Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan in 1632, is the ultimate testament to the brilliance of parchin kari.
An immense mausoleum of white marble, built in Agra between 1631 and 1648 by order of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his favourite wife
they used to be done in 1633, when the 17-year construction of the Taj Mahal began-except that the craft is applied to souvenirs rather than mausoleums these days.
Many of the design elements foreshadow the Taj Mahal, the construction of which began in 1630.
It is believed that more than 20,000 artisans, labourers, painters and others were involved in the construction of the building.
is believed to have employed 20,000 laborers
It eventually took more than 1,000 elephants and 20,000 craftsmen from all over Asia to build (Nath, 1985).

For its construction, masons, stone-cutters, inlayers, carvers, painters, calligraphers, dome builders and other artisans were requisitioned from the whole of the empire and also from the Central Asia and Iran.
the most skilled architects, inlay craftsmen, calligraphers, stone-carvers and masons were called from all across India and lands as distant as Persia and Turkey.
Records indicate that the parchin kari craftsmen were mostly from Kannauj and were not Muslim but Hindus (Havell, 2003).
Two additional tomb buildings, called Saheli Burj, lie along the south end of the complex.

One of the four tombs contains a marble cenotaph embellished with parchin kari (this technique was only used in the tombs of the emperor's family at the time the Taj Mahal was built), but vandals have stolen many of the more valuable inlaid stones.
Humayun, the second Mughal emperor, is credited with introducing inlay as a significant feature of Mughal architecture.
The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque in Delhi's Purana Qila (1540 CE) showcases one of the earliest examples of inlay work in India, with its mihrab adorned with gold and semi-precious stones.
The tomb itself is considered the first Mughal structure in India built entirely of white marble.
It was the first Mughal structure built entirely of white marble, setting the stage for the architectural marvels to come.
The I'timad al-Daula was the first Mughal structure to be completely encased in marble and extensively use pietra dura, the marble inlay work that is associated with the Taj Mahal.
The Tomb of Itimad-Ud-Daula, commissioned by Empress Nur Jahan for her father, for instance, features polychromatic geometric designs, flowers and decorated vases using the technique.
Before the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra (1621-1627 CE) marked a turning point in Mughal architecture.
Floral and stylized arabesques, geometrical designs, opus sectile mosaic and pietra dura inlay are used throughout the exterior.

The mausoleum is like a jewel box: built entirely of pure marble, it marks the transitional phase from the grand and massive red sandstone architecture of Akbar to the softer and sensual architectural style that marked the reign of Shah Jahan.
Before the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra (1621-1627 CE) marked a turning point in Mughal architecture.

It marks a transitional phase in Mughal architecture from the red sandstone and marble decoration of the monuments of Akbar's era, such as Humayun's Tomb and Akbar's tomb, to the white marble and pietra dura inlay exemplified by the Taj Mahal of Shah Jahan.
Before the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra (1621-1627 CE) marked a turning point in Mughal architecture.
His daughter, Nur Jahan, later married the Emperor and commissioned the mausoleum to honor the memory of her father upon his death in 1622.
Built between 1622 and 1628, it was commissioned by the Mughal empress Nur Jahan for her father
It first appeared in Rome in the 16th century, reaching its full maturity in Florence.

The technique of creating inlays from coloured stones was practised by the ancient Romans and revived in the 1550s in Rome, where recent archaeological excavations meant that there were abundant supplies of antique marbles to be found.
Most historians credit the Italians with creating this technique in Florence, where it was called commesso di pietre dure ("composition of hard stones") and often abbreviated to pietra dura
Said to have been originally developed and perfected by Florentine artists in sixteenth-century Italy
The Mughals had received gifts from Italy of decorative objects with inlay and had acquired an appreciation for the art.
European artists brought the technique with them to India to work on the Taj Mahal.
The tradition of fine stone inlay, or parchin kari, developed independently in India and began to be incorporated into the monuments of the Mughal empire during the sixteenth century.
The art of Pietra Dura, as it was called in Italy, was brought to India in the 17th century by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan when he commissioned the Taj Mahal and brought experts from Persia
The art was brought to India in the 17th century from Persia when Shah Jahan chose to build the Taj Mahal.
In the 16th century, this craft journeyed to India, where it underwent a remarkable transformation under Mughal patronage, becoming the uniquely Indian art of parchin kari.
These decorative patterns, found throughout the tomb, were created by adapting the western pietra dura technique, believed to have been imported to the court during the reign of the emperor Jahangir.

Some scholars believe that Italian artisans taught local artisans at Mughal workshops, while others think that local artisans might have learnt it themselves since they were already skilled in inlay techniques that employed softer stones.
While we still do not know which of these versions is true

The decline of Mughal power in the 18th century marked a turning point for parchin kari. As royal patronage waned, artisans began creating decorative items like tabletops and jewelry boxes for European buyers, who were enchanted by the intricate craftsmanship.
The Parchinkari craftsmen of Agra are believed to be descendants of the same craftsmen who built the Taj Mahal.

Fortunately, the artisans were still able to pass on their skills to future generations (although only to the men and only within the family)

Makrana is the oldest among cities in India with marble quarries.

The master artist who is a thoroughly knowledgeable person plans the each design. Marble panel is divided in systematic sections using traditional geometric tools and making final sketch of the selected design on 1:1 Scale.
The entire drawing is traced on a brass sheet, which is cut out accurately by a specialist to make templates of every component of the design.
The craftsman matches the shapes to a brass template.
Which involves choosing a design, setting a colour scheme and tonality of the design and choosing different types of stones based on their shades to be used in the product.
Based on the design, base stones and inlay stones are sourced. The base stone may be white or black marble or soapstone.

In advanced inlays, slivers of different gem materials were artfully placed in the space with a view toward creating colors and shapes of the desired geometric patterns or floral designs. A bow saw coated with abrasives was used to fashion the slivers (figure 19).

The stone to be inlayed are cut and given the desired shape as per the design using a special instrument called emery wheel. Since each part of the design is shaped individually, it is time consuming.
Stone slivers are carefully shaped into minute petals, leaves, and stems on a manually operated emery wheel.
Each shape is ground individually and must fit precisely without any gaps.
This begins with lapidary artists who shape the selected gem stones on a hand driven tool known as "Saan & Kamaani".
tiny pieces of gemstones are held in the fingertips and touched with emery wheel, which is rotated by hand with great precision using a cane rod attached with a leather band.
On a recent trip to India, I had the chance to learn how these stone inlays are made.
The artisans work together as a cooperative, meaning each of them remains an individual artist with complete creative freedom, but all profits are shared equally.
The starting point are thin sheets of various (semiprecious) stone, from which the artisan creates delicate shapes, some only a few millimetres in size
Only a (human-powered) grindstone is used
Each shape is ground individually and must fit precisely without any gaps.
A master artist known as the parchinkar would first draw the pattern in henna dye on the marble's surface.
Once a perfect fit has been achieved, the marble plate, into which the ornamental pattern will be integrated, is covered with a layer of henna paint.

The single pieces that make the inlay pattern are laid out on the marble plate and their outlines scratched into the surface. The orange color serves as an orientation when carving out the individual grooves, into which the semiprecious stone pieces will be glued.
Craftsmen trace the design onto the base stone using a sharp tool.
Grooves are cut into the design in the base stone using a chisel such that the shaped stone can perfectly fit in them.
Artisans, known as parachinkars, carve intricate grooves into marble, into which semi-precious stones are carefully inlaid.
To make a marble inlay artefact, the stones are cut and shaped with a hand-operated machine while the marble is chiselled with a diamond-tipped chisel.
Once the grooves are cut, the stones are inlayed into the base stone using glue. Traditional methods like charcoal or modern methods like araldite are being used.
The stone is then pressed into place and fixed with a burning charcoal.
the glue in use is still a paste made from sugar cane, bees wax, honey, lemon juice, marble dust and lentils.
Then the artist would carve out a space in the marble and fill it with thin polished pieces of gem materials, affixing them with organic glue.
The stones were grooved so they would fit together, making the contact between them almost invisible. The technique is still used to this day
held in place using an adhesive (the exact recipe for which is hard to figure out. It&rsquos a trade secret, the artisans claim)
Once inlayed, the stones need to be left for some time for drying so that they are properly pasted.
Hand polishing of the base article is done using a traditional polishing powder which is applied on the surface with a soft moist muslin cloth.
The final polishing is done using zink powder.
The final polishing is done with zinc power.
Grinding and polishing is a multi stage process, using graded grit of hard stone, followed by continuous rubbing with pigments and wax.
A grind stone shard is used to smoothen the surface after the inlays have been inserted.
The henna paint is also removed during this smoothening process. The inlay piece is now properly integrated into the marble plate, and gets a final finish with a layer of wax.
There are two categories of artisans- Sadakars and Pachikars.

While basic cutting and carving aided by machines is done by skilled Sadakars, exclusive inlay work, requiring the expertise similar to cutting and polishing of jewelry stones using chisels and grinding stones is done by experienced Pachikars.

Artisans operating with country-made machines for cutting, grinding, buffing and polishing of stone. In spite of the use of these simple machines, it requires a very skillful manipulation of chisel and hammer to bring out curvilinear patterns and designs.
Latest water jet cutting technology is used to get intricate and detailed work. There are experts who can produce marble inlay work to CAD or Printing Drawings.
Flat Chisel (chheeni): It is used to carve out the fine details on the surface of the marble.
Cold Chisel (tanki): It helps to cut through the raw marble slab to get the basic shape of the desired product
Hammer (hatora): This tool is used to drive the chisel through the raw marble for both sculpting and carving.
Pen Drill (barma): It is used to make rough outlines of the patterns on the surface of the marble
This tool is also used for carving the designs.
Divider (prakaar): To draw outlines in the form of concentric circles for geometric patterns.

Carnelian (Red-Orange) Known for its bright reddish-orange color, carnelian is often used in floral patterns.
Malachite (Green) A striking green stone often used for its deep, swirling patterns.
Coral (Red or Pink) A vibrant red or pink organic material often used for accenting inlay designs.
Jasper (Varied Colors) Jasper stones come in various colors such as red, yellow, green, and brown and are often used in more earthy tones in the inlay work.

Makrana Marble is calcitic marble from the Makrana and Parbatsar Tehsils (Makrana Region) of Nagaur District of Rajasthan
Makrana marble is calcitic marble. It is known for the best quality monumental marble, comparable to world famous marbles of Carrara, Italy and Pentelinkar, Greece.
Of this only Makrana Marble from Nagaur District and Sirohi Marble from Sirohi District are the calcitic marbles. All other marbles in India are dolomitic marble.
the calcium carbonate content in it is more than 98% and the presence of impurities/ other constituents such as magnesium oxide, iron oxide, silica, aluminia, sulpher etc are less than 2%.
That apart, the Calcium Oxide content upon combustion is 50- 56 which is the highest among marbles.
The Makrana marble has made a perceptible dent in marble industry because of its blockability, whiteness, high CaO 50-56 %, low MgO 0.90-1.77 %, as compared to other marbles of Rajasthan
While magnesium and iron content is negligent.

Because of which it retains its white color (original color) for hundreds of years, while other marble stone change color from white to grey, black or yellow shade due to the oxidization of Magnesium and iron respectively over the years to their respective oxides.
According to the presence of impurities / other constituents the shade / colour of Makrana Marble varies from pure shades of white to white with grey / pink shades across.
This interlocking of grains also give it strength, hardness and translucency.
The water absorption of Makrana Marble is 0.04%, which is again the lowest among all calcitic marbles.
Makrana Marble is on the whole harder than marbles imported from Greece and Italy and is consequently more resistant to abrasion.
It is also very easy to work with as it has no free silica which may be hard on tools or interfere with polishing.
Makrana marble deposits belong to the Ajmer Formation of the Kumbhalgarh Group of the Delhi Supergroup
They form part of the Ajmer Formation of the Delhi Supergroup, which is a sequence of sedimentary rocks that was deposited in the Delhi Basin during the Proterozoic.

About 1450 Ma (million years ago) these rocks were affected by the Delhi Orogeny, causing the metamorphism that transformed the original limestones to marble and the folding that caused the steep dip and the current outcrop pattern.
The different marble bands have formed due to tight isoclinal folding
